ety.text: From Middle English riot (“debauched living, dissipation”), from Old French riote (“debate”), from rioter (“to quarrel”), perhaps related to riboter or from Latin rugio (“to roar”). Compare French riotte and Occitan riòta.

senses.d: A tumultuous disturbance of the public peace by a large group of people, often involving violence or damage to property.
ex: The protests began peacefully but turned into riots after several days.
In summer this flower garden is a riot of colour.

senses.d: A humorous or entertaining event or person.
ex: Check this out! We have to get this! I can't believe all this stuff! This is a total riot!
They call me "quiet girl", but I'm a riot

senses.d: Wanton or unrestrained behavior or emotion.
ex: For when his head-ſtrong Riot hath no Curbe,

senses.d: Excessive and expensive feasting; wild and loose festivity; revelry.
ex: the lamb thy riot dooms to bleed to-day

senses.d: To create or take part in a riot; to raise an uproar or sedition.
ex: The nuclear protesters rioted outside the military base.

senses.d: To act in an unrestrained or wanton manner; to indulge in excess of feasting, luxury, etc.
ex: Now he exact of all, wastes in delight, / Riots in pleasure, and neglects the law.

senses.d: To cause to riot; to throw into a tumult.

grp.label: to create or take part in a riot

ety.text: From the old past participle of émouvoir (“to move emotionally”), influenced by meute (“pack (of hounds)”).

Maybe from Latin Bacchānālia (“feast of Bacchus”), plural of Bacchānal (“a place devoted to Bacchus”), from Bacchus (“the god of wine”), from Ancient Greek Βάκχος (Bákkhos). Compare with French boucan.
